utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, are you ready? I believe you concluded the direction of Dr. Gow ---

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- yesterday evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is right, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Will you present Dr. Gow for cross-examination though, will you?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I sincerely so. DR. JAMES GOW, recalled.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You may be seated, Dr. Gow. You understand you are still under oath, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: The passing of time, Dr. Gow, has reduced my questions from two to one, but whoever was the last Federal Prime Minister of Yugoslavia, whether it was Markovic or Panic, I am not quite sure which?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The last Prime Minister of the SFRY was Ante Markovic. Milan Panic was later to be the Prime Minister of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that is, Serbia and Montenegro declared after 27th April 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I think it is in relation to Panic, what has been the situation since Panic's time as far as the federal organisation of Serbia and Montenegro? I take it that there is a Federal Executive as well as two Republican Executives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There are federal bodies in Serbia and Montenegro. Most observers would judge that the Federation has little meaning other than to serve the interest of Belgrade in pursuing the question of succession to the SFRY by keeping to the name. The position of Montenegro within the Federation is characterised by a degree of friction, in recent times there were a series of inter-republican trade difficulties -- trade war might be excessive. Montenegro remains part of the Federation but, as one Yugoslav official characterised it to me, the Federation is 95 per cent Serbia. It is significant that it was the Serbian President, Slobodan Milosevic, who represented the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, for example, in the Dayton talks at Wright Paterson air base rather than the Federal officials.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Is there a Federal President and a Federal Prime Minister?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is -- both of those officers exist, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: But they are relatively insignificant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are relatively insignificant in terms of the exercise of political power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, you have mentioned that when the Royal Dictatorship was created in 1929, there was also the creation of a province called Croatian Banovina; is there any significance in the word "banovina"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I could first correct your understanding. I think the record would show that I said that the Croatian Banovina was created in 1939, not in 1929 when the Royal Dictatorship was proclaimed. The significance in the "banovina" is the word "ban". It is an old word meaning something like "duke", and it had significance for Croatians within the Hungarian sphere of the Austro-Hungarian Empire and going back to the ideas of Croatian statehood and monarchy. There had been a Croatian kingdom in the Middle Ages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, have you concluded your direct examination of Dr. Gow?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Orie, will you conduct the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, I would first like to tell you that I am not a native English speaker, so if there is anything unclear in what I ask you, would you please ask me to clarify myself so that there will be no misunderstandings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would do so indeed, though I very much doubt it would happen. My experience of people from the Netherlands is that they speak far better English than people from my own country.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I was not fishing for any compliments but, nevertheless, thank you very much! Dr. Gow, you told the Chamber that you had some knowledge of the Serbo Croatian language and of the Slovene language. Could you please tell us more precisely how far your knowledge of these languages go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say that I have a functional working knowledge of these languages. I have used those languages in carrying out research in the course of doing a doctorate and in subsequent employment as an academic. I use it to go to talk to officials and military people working in the countries of the former Yugoslavia and previously in the SFRY as it was. I use the characterisation "some knowledge" not to give any impression that I would regard myself as having complete competence and fluency in using the language, but I have a knowledge of the language which is adequate for me to carry out my work and which I have used in the course of my career.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gow. Did you ever make any translation of documents for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not made formal translations of documents for the Prosecution. I have brought to the attention of the Prosecution documents published, published documents, and I have translated them informally for the Office of the Prosecutor. The Office of the Prosecutor has then used translators to make the translations which it would use for purposes of its work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, did you ever draw the attention to documents that were already translated to the Prosecution, translated in English, I mean to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because I drew their attention, for example, to documents from the Yugoslav survey which was submitted in evidence yesterday. I may have drawn their attention to other documents which were already translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Did you check when you drew their attention to English text whether the translation was correct or was not correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think your question is did I ever -- this may be a question of language -- did I ever check; the answer is yes, there would be occasions on which I did check but it was not the case that I would always check.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gow. Did you visit the area of the Opstina of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not. I have never been in the area of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: You have never been in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have never been in the area of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gow. May I refer to an answer you gave when Exhibit 51 was shown to you, that is the constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina of 28th February 1992? Judge Stephen asked you yesterday whether that constitution designated a capital, Knin, Sarajevo; you replied that you thought it did not designate a capital. Could you please, with the help of the Registry, look again at Exhibit 51, look carefully to it and see whether it designates a capital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Handed) If I could make one small point of clarification, if not correction? I believe yesterday I said I did not recall if this was the case. I was also prepared to say, on the basis of reflection last night, that the claim was made to the capital being in Sarajevo and discussions had taken place about dividing Sarajevo. If you look at Article 9, you will see that Sarajevo is designated to be the capital of the Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: So it is in the constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is in the constitution that the Republika Srpska, or in this case it was still the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, sought to establish Sarajevo, or part of Sarajevo, as its capital.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I ask you, Dr. Gow, whether this part is properly translated in that part of the Exhibit that gives the English text?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to say that Article 9 does not appear at all on the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gow. So the English text does not say anything about the capital and original text does?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The original text does. The English translation does not have an Article 9 in which reference to the capital is made.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Dr. Gow. Dr. Gow, on 7th May, you testified on the subject of movements of population. You testified on the basis of Exhibit 7, I think. Could we please have Exhibit 7 available for the witness? (Handed) I do not know whether if it could be put on the screen? That is fine, as far as I am concerned. So, Dr. Gow, when speaking about the movement of populations, you have drawn our attention to northern Bosnia which is part of this Exhibit. Could you please look with me at some other areas as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please look at Tuzla and see whether there was a significant movement of Serb population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was, indeed, a significant move of the Serbian population out of the area of Tuzla. You can see that it was reduced to around, in broad terms, a quarter of its 1991 level. At the same time you will see approximately a doubling of the Muslim population. This is based on overall the displacement of populations within the areas. If you were to look at western Herzegovina as well, you would see a similar effect with the Serbian population being reduced from 43,500 only to 5,000, at the same time seeing a significant increase in the Muslim population in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please have a look at Bihac? Was there a significant reduction of Serb population over there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again you will see that there was a significant reduction in the Serbian population in the Bihac area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Was there a significant reduction of the Serbian population in the Zenica area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again you will see a significant reduction in the population of the Serbs in the area around Zenica, and a lesser reduction in the area of the Croat population and a growth of around 100,000 in the Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, could you please tell us where these Serbian people moved to? The Serbian people I am talking about of the Tuzla area, the Bihac area, the Zenica area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think anybody would be able to tell you exactly where all of them moved. In general, I think it is fair to say that they moved either into the areas indicated on the schedule in which you have a growth of Serbian population, or they moved to the territory of Serbian and Montenegro. In the period of this schedule, there may have been around, my recollection is not precise, but I think somewhere in the region of several hundred thousand, maybe 5,000, 6,000, refugees in Serbia and Montenegro from Croatia and Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, so you say no-one could tell us where exactly these people went?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think that anybody could tell you exactly where all those people went. I think if you were to go to representatives of humanitarian organisations, particularly the United Nations High Commission for Refugees, they would be in a position on the basis of the kind of data they collect as represented in this schedule to give you a more precise answer than I would be able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, if they would have to carry out such an investigation, would you not need, at least, to know which people were in the census figures because the first are prewar figures, as far as I can see, are census figures --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: -- and the other ones are UNHCR refugee figures. Is it known exactly, let us say in western Bosnia, 304,000 Serbs, who they were exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The UNHCR, as far as I am aware and as far as it possibly can, forms registers of people and to report to the -----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I am talking about the prewar situation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, sorry. There would have been a register of citizens for the census to be taken and, therefore, I assume that there would be some record of who was there. That record, I would not know if that record would indicate individual names by designated ethnic grouping. So whether or not there is a record in the federal statistical office in Belgrade or anywhere else of an individual's name being against their declared ethnic national grouping.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Is my understanding then right that this investigation could not successfully be done because no names of the census can be linked with the census figures from the prewar period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I am not sure what the question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I asked you whether it was known where these people went. I understood your answer saying that the UNHCR might do because they have lists of names. Then I asked you whether there were lists of names of the prewar period because I think you would need both of them in order to find out where they were and where they are now. I also do understand that you answered to that question that it is at least uncertain whether these names of the prewar period are known or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I answered that it was uncertain, or I am unaware, if those names are known and are connected with the designation of ethno-national groupings anywhere. I am not sure that I follow the logic of the question; maybe I just do not understand it. It seems to me that for the purposes of the evidence being given, there is a broad indication of population movements. As a broad indication, I do not think that tracking the record of every individual would be necessary. I stand to be corrected if that would be the case. I certainly would also direct you to the possibility that when organisations such as the UNHCR take records of this kind, they very often, if not always, ask people for the locations from which they have come. So I believe they would have some indication. I do not have knowledge of what that would be and I cannot be certain that they do have it, but I would judge that it is likely that they might.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Let me put a question very briefly. Is there a cross-reference of names known between 1991 and 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any cross-reference of names known between 1991 and 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I am not sure what the question is again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Whether there is any cross-reference, as far as names are concerned, between the prewar figures and the July 1994 figures?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: When you have numbers, for example, in Tuzla you have Serbs 82,235, do you have names in addition to the numbers to reflect so that you can determine who is who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do I have the names?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Does one have names? Are they available, to your knowledge? I do not think you would have them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have them and I do not have knowledge whether or not they are available.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gow. Dr. Gow, you testified when you were asked about the movement of the population that it was mainly a movement of Muslim population. You said that although other people moved as well, Serbs, Croats, the number and the scale were different where the movement of Muslim people were involved. Could you please give us those numbers of movement of Muslim people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The total figures for displaced people, as far as I recall, in a period 1993/94 were around 2.7 million -- I am trying hard to remember the figures , and my recollection would be that perhaps half, a little over half that figure would be Muslims, but I do not have exact figures from the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: If you are talking about figures, are you talking about absolute figures or are you talking about relative figures, compared to the part of the population of those Muslims or Croats or Serbs were within that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The figure to which I just made reference, as far as with my memory I can be sure of it, was reference to an absolute figure. The UNHCR reported, my recollection was, dealing with 2.7 million people -- I cannot be sure that my memory is correct on that -- and I think that around half, slightly over half, of those would be Muslims, so it is an absolute figure, not a proportional figure. The slightly half or slightly over half, if I am correct on that, is a proportion of the 2.7 million, if I am correct on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us how the remaining 50 per cent, were they Serbs, were they Croats, were they both of them, were they equally divided among the other 50 per cent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot tell you. I cannot give you an exact or even what I would regard as a reliable approximate indication. My judgment would be that , it is very difficult to say , numbers of Serbs did move out of areas in earlier parts of the war and right at the end in 1993 numbers of Croats were moving from central Bosnia. Because I have not checked it, I would not give you, I would not want to give you any attempt at an exact figure on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, could you then please explain again how you could tell us that the scale of the movement of Muslims was different from any of the other groups because, as far as I understand, you now say a vague recollection might be 50 per cent, but you do not know how the other 50 per cent, whether these were Serbs, Croats. Could you then please explain why the scale is different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The scale is different because the largest number of those involved were from Muslim communities, as I think was just indicated, and I say these things on the basis, not of having checked the records, but on the basis of extensive observation over the past few years and of talking with officials of various international organisations, including the United Nations High Commission for Refugees, but I am afraid I am not in a position here and now without further preparation to go beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Did they give you figures or did they give you impressions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They gave both figures and impressions. You will see that some figures are presented here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Let me go to these figures you have presented, Dr. Gow. If I look at that part of your exhibit that is giving numbers and where not mixed is added, because I have some difficulties in seeing what happens to people if they finally are part of a mixed population, because it is difficult to see exactly what then happens. If I look at the other figures, so leaving out Sarajevo and the Enclaves and the eastern Bosnia, could you give us a rough idea on how many people moved out and in and what, for example, I just ask the question to you whether there is any important difference between the movements of Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, is there an important difference between the movement of Muslims and Croats; is that the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: If I see how many people move out, how many people move in, because we do not know whether they are the same people or not, so let us look at the balance, the final balance, of those figures apart from Sarajevo and the Enclaves and eastern Bosnia, how many people are finally missing or are extra at the end?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I am not sure what you are asking me again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I will try to explain to you again. If you use these figures, you could calculate at the end how many people left the whole area that is described in the schedule and how many were extra there at the end?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are asking me to, I am sorry, if I can be clearer, is it right that I am being asked to perform an arithmetical exercise?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, as a matter of fact, if you could please follow me. Of course, I have tried to calculate already, and I have come to a deficit of 250,000 Muslims approximately, not precise, 2,000 or 3,000, and Croats is 175,000. Can you follow this? I really try to do my best.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: OK. Would it be possible for me to take it as a whole?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand what your problem is. Perhaps it is good if I just give you the figures on which I based my calculation. I am starting with the Muslims, western Bosnia, minus 250,000; then western Herzegovina, minus 70,000; Zenica, a surplus of 100,000; Tuzla, a surplus of 285,000; northern Bosnia, minus 350,000; Bihac is approximately equal. That makes minus 250,000. If I now look at the Croats: I see western Bosnia, approximately minus 30,000; western Herzegovina, plus 55,000; Zenica, minus 50,000; Tuzla, approximately equal; northern Bosnia, minus 150,000; Bihac approximately equal. If you add that, it would come to 250,000 Muslims ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And 175,000 Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: -- minus 250,000 Muslims and minus 175,000 Croats. Dr. Gow, are you aware of the spread of Muslims and Croats in the population of the area to which this exhibit relates? What is the division of Croats/Muslims in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I need to be clear what you are asking me again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: We talked about several regions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell me what was the percentage, from an ethnical point of view, of the population of this area in '91?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The area, if the area is the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, then the share of Croats, as far as I recall, was around 17 per cent and the share of Muslims was 44 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you compare these percentages to the total number of people that moved out, if you are relating to it, would you say that the final result of the Muslims leaving the area, well, missing the area in the end -- we do not know where they have gone -- is significantly less from a proportionate point of view or is it significantly more or is it equal? So we have minus 250,000 Muslims on 44 per cent of the population and we have minus 170,000 on 17 per cent of the population. Could you please give your opinion on the proportion of people that moved out related to their proportion in the population at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As an academic specialising in war studies rather than arithmetics, I can give you my impression which is that 170,000 would be a greater proportion of something which was expressed as 17 per cent than 250,000 as a proportion of something expressed as 44 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But maybe there are people with better arithmetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: That answers my question, Dr. Gow. Dr. Gow, a memorandum of the Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences was produced as an exhibit in court on Wednesday. Why did you judge the version you were talking about then to be a more authoritative version? That is what you told us.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is that Exhibit 21, Mr. Orie?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, it is Exhibit 21. I am not going into the content of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My judgment that it was more authoritative was based on two things: One is on my sense of what the document, with what the document was concerned and the context in which it was made and the way in which that, rather than other versions of the document which I have seen, seems more properly and, indeed, moderately to correspond with the issues under discussion; the second is on the basis of discussions with academics in Belgrade, some of whom were aware of the document at the time it was being based such as, if I can indicate, Professor Svetozar Stojanivic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please tell me exactly what means authoritative?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My use of the term "authoritative" in this way was not to indicate that it had the authority of the Academy because I think I gave indication that the Academy is of the opinion that there was never an official document nothing more than a document of a discussion group. I used the sense "authoritative" to mean the one which most correctly reflected the concerns of the authors of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: What is the basis on which you know exactly what is the concern of this small working group of people that worked on one of the versions of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe I already answered the question, but I am happy to do it again, which is that on my sense of the issues that were being discussed and having seen in the past two other versions of it, or two other documents purporting to be versions of it, and also on the basis of talking to academics in Belgrade, including Professor Svetozar Stojanivic who was at times close to and associated with some of the people who were said to be involved in preparing the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time you said, Dr. Gow, that the document may not be authoritative. I mean, how do I have to understand, on the one hand, you say the document is more authoritative and, on the other hand, you say it may not be authoritative?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, I think I just indicated the response to that but I am happy to do so again. I use the term, if I use the term ----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: If I may interrupt you, perhaps to clarify the question, you are talking about the same document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: You first said that it may not be authoritative and then a few lines later you say that it is more authoritative.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I can clarify? Forgive my use of English; it is obviously another case in which your use of English as a Dutchman is far superior to that of a native speaker. The original use of "authoritative", as I was indicating in my response a moment ago, was to say that it is my understanding that the Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences does not regard it as an official, as an authoritative document of the Academy. The second use of "authoritative" and the "more authoritative" was not by reference to the statement, it is not regarded as authoritative, but by reference to documents which I have seen purporting to be other versions of it. Therefore, I am saying that I think the version which was used is one which can give a fair indication of the concerns of whoever the members of the group in the Serbian Academy of Sciences were of the situation in Serbia and Yugoslavia at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Did the other version that you saw not reflect what was your idea of what the issues were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The other documents which I have seen certainly reflected the concerns. My assessment of one them is now a long time ago, and I have to say that I cannot recall precisely the details of it, one of the others which I have seen seems to me to go beyond a degree of moderation which is expressed in this document in terms of the use of language, the concerns are the same. It is, therefore, for that reason that I think this document would be the one that I would choose to use as an example rather than a document which might be more -- might be less reasoned. I am not sure if I am using the right words again, but I am trying to give a reasonable indication of how I see the version of the document which was presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gow. I do understand you prefer this version of the document. Dr. Gow, I would like to ask a few questions on constitutional matters. I would like to start with the Federative Yugoslav constitution. You have stated that in the Yugoslav constitution of 1974 the right to self-determination was embodied in the preamble. The preamble you were referring to on page 5 of Exhibit 19? I will ask the Registry to provide you with Exhibit 19. (Handed)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I do not know whether you still can read it if it is on the display, but I do not want to prevent you from reading it. Is the preamble you were referring to the one on page 5 of Exhibit 19?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I refer to it as a preamble; it is here labelled "introductory part," but that is the thing to which I was making reference, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, is the right to self-determination, including the right to secession, mentioned at any other point in this constitution apart from this preamble?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure. I cannot say that it is or is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: You do not know whether it is anywhere else in the constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall. I have looked through the constitution. I do not know if I have ever read every last word of it, and I certainly do not recall if it appears anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: What is meant in this the preamble by the term "the nations of Yugoslavia"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The term "nations of Yugoslavia"-- from the original in Serbo-Croat, the nation, "narod" -- is used in two senses. In one sense, it is used to imply, if not clearly indicate, the state forming peoples -----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I did not understand this part of your answers. Would you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The whole?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: No, you started with telling me it was in two sense, you said, and then I could not understand you from that moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: OK. I think that the term "nation" is used in two senses. In Serbo-Croat the word "narod" means both "nation" and "people" and I would regard them, in my judgment, from a political point of view looking at these things in the context of either studied politics or international relations, there is degree of ambiguity and one which I think may have put there expressly by those involved in Yugoslavia. The term "nation", "narod" means both "people" and "nation" in Serbo-Croat. The term "nation" is used to imply, if not clearly to indicate, reference to those state forming peoples of the SFRY, of the territories of SFRY. So I think we discussed this when I was giving evidence, the first part of my evidence. So, Serbs, Croats, Slovenes and so forth would be regarded as state forming peoples. But the use of "nations" is also drawn from the language of international relations and in the sense of "peoples", because in international documentation, in international politics, the right to self-determination inheres with peoples rather than with ethno-national groups in the sense of state forming peoples. It is a complex discussion which takes place among academics and, in practice, the term, leaving aside the wording here, or in any other part of the constitution if it appears somewhere else, but in practical terms the right to self-determination, here labelled the right of every nation to self-determination, is in fact, as per my understanding, in international documentation and in practice -- sorry, in practice in accordance, as far as it is in accordance, with international documents is given to peoples, and "peoples" have always been interpreted as those inhabiting designated territories, usually with a quality of sovereignty or something like that. So, in the whole process of decolonization in the UN era, the right to self-determination was granted to the inhabitants of all the territories in the formal colonial areas, rather than, for example, to the particular ethno-national groups in any of the post colonial countries; one of the reasons why, you may suppose, there are a lot of intercommunal conflicts in many of the post colonial countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, is not the word "the nations of Yugoslavia" in this preamble compared and contrasted with nationalities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: It does not make that clear what is meant by "nation" in this preamble, since I do not understand from your testimony that nationality means to say national minorities. That is the explanation you gave of the word "nationality" on 8th May.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, could you repeat the question? I think I lost it by the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: My question was whether "nation" is not compared and contrasted with nationalities in this preamble; I think your answer was that it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The word "nationality" appears, yes. If you look approximately halfway through the first paragraph, you will see the original reference to "nations" or "peoples". It continues after the word, after the phrase, "common interest", "together with nationalities".

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Could there then still be any ambiguity as to the meaning of the word "nation" here, where it is compared to the national minorities, could it refer to state? You indicated that in other countries, perhaps even in other continents, they have their own developments in their self-determination, but I would like to stick to this preamble where the nations of Yugoslavia are mentioned, compared to and contrasted to nationalities. Could it then have any other meaning than the major south Slav groups in Yugoslavia, that means Croats, Macedonians, Montenegrins, Muslims, Serbs and Slovenes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In juxtaposition, the use of the terms "nations" and "nationalities" in the Yugoslav context is there to indicate the difference between those groups labelled as nations, state forming peoples, the ones to which you made reference, and other groups. I was indicating previously that there is a degree of ambiguity because the use of the phrase "right of every nation to self-determination", because the word is the same in Serbo-Croat, creates a degree of ambiguity because the two senses are elided in one. The right to self-determination for peoples may also applied theoretically, I am sure, to ethno-national groups; I simply said, in practice, has always been applied, as far as I am aware (and certainly in the UN era), to territories rather than to ethno-national groups. So it is an ambiguous use of terminology. In one sense, in the first clause, the use of "nations of Yugoslavia", I think, is probably because it is juxtaposed with nationalities can be taken in the sense of the state forming ethno-national groups, but placing the same word in the next line creates an ambiguity in terms of the understanding of international relations, as far as I see these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I am talking about constitutional aspects, not about the international complications of it. Could you then please read it aloud for us so that we all know exactly where in your vision the ambiguity might be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do you wish me to?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: To read the preamble, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The whole of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I would like you to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "The nations of Yugoslavia. Proceeding from the right of every nation to self-determination, including the right to secession on the basis of their will freely expressed in the common struggle of all nations and nationalities in the national liberation war and socialist revolution, and in conformity with their historic aspirations, aware that further consolidation of their brotherhood and unity is in the common interest, have together with the nationalities with which they live united in a Federal Republic of free and equal nations and nationalities and founded on a Socialist Federal community of working people, the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, in which in the interests of each nation and nationalities separately and of all of them together they shall realise and ensure" -- do you wish me to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gow. Were the Muslim Slavs in Bosnia a state forming people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By the time of the 1974 constitution, they were qualified as being one of the nations of Yugoslavia. At the end of the Second World War -- indeed, I suppose, during the course of the Second World War -- there was some discussion about the position of the Slav Muslims, but at that stage they were not treated as one of nations, a state forming peoples. In the course of the 1960s, the question of their position was raised again and I think by 1968 within Party documents they were being identified as one of the nations in this use of the term. When the 1974 constitution was introduced, by that time they were regarded as one of the nations of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: My final question, did they have their own state, the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: The answer is no, thank you, Dr. Gow. Are the republics of Yugoslavia given the right to secede from the Yugoslav Federation under this constitution? I am talking about the republics, not about people's republics.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The republics are not given the right explicitly to leave the Federation, although throughout all the constitutions the federations were unions of the republics, and the republics were the political, territorial entities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but the answer is no, the republics as such were not given the right to secede?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The republics were not explicitly given the right to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: That answers my question, Dr. Gow. In view of the fact that the republics were not explicitly given the right to secede under the 1974 constitution, was opposition to secession upholding the lawful constitution? So if you were to oppose against the secession, would this be upholding the lawful constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a very complex and ambiguous area. Again, it goes back to the ambiguous use of the word "narod" eliding two senses of the use of the term. There was an understanding in the philosophy of the evolution of these republics and the way they evolved during the Second World War as the regional councils of the Anti-Fascist, Council of the National Liberation of Yugoslavia, that they were at one level intended to convey or confer statehood on the state forming peoples as understood in the course of the Second World War, and the right to self-determination was used in a rather ambiguous way; again, the two senses which I have described being brought together. Although there was no explicit right to session, as far as I am aware, given to the republics, the republics were deemed to be the constitutional units forming the Federation in 1946 and afterwards, and in terms of the application of the principle of self-determination in practice in international relations, it would conventionally be the case that it would be the political territorial communities which would have the right to exercise this right rather than an ethno-national grouping. The Yugoslavs in drafting these constitutions, I believe, were explicitly trying to have it both ways in order to address two different questions within the context of the complex federation that the SFRY and its predecessors, the Federal People's Republic of Yugoslavia, was. Therefore, although there was no explicit right to secession, the right to self-determination was a matter of interpretation and application and, in practice, could only be put into effect by political territorial communities. To oppose secession of a republic, if secession was being sought, would be an appropriate action, because I think I made reference to Article 5 of the constitution which indicated that changes could only be made with the agreement of all the states forming the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: So opposition to secession was upholding the constitution, that was my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Am I right, Dr. Gow, when I said that you stated that in the free elections of 1990 nationalist party have won in all republics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would probably have to check the record to be sure whether or not you are right in saying that. I think that I said that in Slovenia, nationalist parties and reformed communists with a nationalist agenda won the elections, something like this. In Croatia, nationalist parties won the elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the vote mostly went along the lines of national party divisions; in Serbia and Montenegro, communists or reformed communists with nationalist platforms won the elections. I did not mention Macedonia, I believe, but in Macedonia again there was a strong nationalist dimension with some form of communists and some nationalists being successful in the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Did the Yugoslav Federal constitution guarantee the equal rights of citizens?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know where it does that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the 1989 amendment to the Slovenia constitution -- I am not talking about the Federal constitution any more -- violate this provision of the Federal constitution by giving ethnic Slovenes superior rights over other citizens of Yugoslavia in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure to which provision you make reference, and I guess that even if I were, I would not be in a position to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Then I perhaps leave this for the time being and see whether I can provide you with the text, although you indicated you could not perhaps even answer to this question. Did the 1990 Croatian constitution, not Slovenia any more, give superior rights to ethnic Croats over other citizens of Yugoslavia in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not be sure if it gave superior rights to ethnic Croats, but it certainly changed the status of ethnic Serbs in a formal sense within the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: In what sense?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe I said this in evidence already, but the 1990 constitution of the Republic of Croatia changed the designation of the Republic of Croatia from being the state of the Croat and Serb peoples and others to being the state of the Croat people and the Serbs and others. So, therefore, the Serbs were moved from being in the first clause as peoples to being in the second clause at the head of a list of Serbs and others. I believe I said that in evidence the other day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: So they were downgraded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly, in terms of that labelling there was a change in status. I think I also said already that was a matter of concern for Serbian people in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you know whether the citizenship laws of Croatia discriminated against non-Croatians, so it is not a constitution but a -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am afraid I have no expertise in citizenship provisions or laws whatsoever, and limited knowledge of citizenship provisions for my own country.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Bearing this in mind, we just discussed, was it reasonable for non-Croats in Croatia in 1991 to fear that they would face discrimination in an independent nationalist Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The weight of your question goes to the word "reasonable", and that would create a number of difficulties. It would on one level, because of the historical experience, nobody could say that nobody who lived in a Serb community where terrible things had happened during the Ustasha regime in the 1940s lived could not have in the back of their mind some memory which might give them concern. At the same time, the weight of your question goes to "reasonable", the word "reasonable. That must be taken on an evaluation of the situation. I would have thought that it would be very difficult to give an absolutely fair judgment on that. Yes, there would be reason for people to have something in the back of their mind, but whether it was reasonable to have substantial fear, I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I did not ask whether they had substantial fear; I asked whether it was reasonable for non-Croats in Croatia to fear that they would face discrimination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, the weight goes to "reasonable". It was not the case that there was no reason for them to have some concern; whether or not it was reasonable for them to fear discrimination is something which, I guess, I would have to go away and think about a lot and research. It is a very difficult kind of question. Certainly, it is the case that there could be some reason for them to have concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I put the question another way: Dr. Gow, if you would be down-graded to a second class citizen, would you fear to be discriminated, either in the back of your mind or -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sure that would depend on the nature and context of the situation. I am not sure what it entails to be downgraded to a second class citizen. I can imagine what it would be to be not a British citizen but a British citizen in dependent territories, for example, but that would be because I was coming from a different area, a different part of the world, and my status and my rights to residency in the United Kingdom would be different. I am not sure within the boundaries of one country how that would work, and how you would label different classes of citizenship. As far as I am aware, there was not a process of labelling different classes of citizenship, but that is only as far as I am aware in this situation in Croatia in which I think you are interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gow. Dr. Gow, since the 1974 Federal Yugoslav constitution does refer to the nations of Yugoslavia as having the right to secede and does not grant explicitly the right to republics, is the argument that areas where a majority population of one of these nations might secede from a republic that claimed the right to secede to form a new nation state for its majority necessarily illegitimate -- I am not clear, I am afraid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not just me then!

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: You will see my first remark was not without reason. I will try to rephrase my question. Dr. Gow, I would like to take you to Exhibit 24. I ask you whether we can put in context your remarks concerning the break up of the former Yugoslavia. Perhaps we can first have Exhibit 24? I would like to put in context your remarks concerning the preparation by Serbia for the break up of the former Yugoslavia. Is it not correct that approximately one year before, in 1989, Slovenia, before any amendment by Serbia, had already amended its constitution to assert the primacy of its own constitutional provisions above those of the Federal constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is my recollection that in 1989, if perhaps not already in 1988, but my memory is not precise, the Republic of Slovenia began -- in the Republic of Slovenia the parliament began a series of acts of legislation which would affirm, if not enhance, the sovereignty of the Republic of Slovenia as one of the states of the SFRY. If it were to be in 1988 (and my memory is not precise), but it did, if not in 1989, it began this process of affirming sovereignty and making changes to its constitution, but if it was in 1989, then I would also point to the fact that although you refer me now to the 1990 constitution of the Republic of Serbia, in the course of giving evidence I did make reference to the amendments that the Republic of Serbia was making to its constitution in 1989. So, to say that it was a year before would be inappropriate; it was a year before the Republic of Serbia adopted a new constitution, but it was at the same time that the Republic of Serbia was adopting its own constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: What did they include, these amendments, exactly, because I would like to compare them with the amendments made in Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The amendments in both cases were concerned with affirming the sovereignty of the two republics. In the case of the amendments (which I believe I have discussed) the Republic of Serbia was seeking to strengthen the quality of, if you can strengthen the quality of sovereignty, I am not sure, but strengthen the reality of the exercise of its sovereign rights as a state by seeking to remove the powers of the two autonomous provinces which impaired the sovereignty in the eyes of those authorities. So, in both cases and in the case of the Republic of Slovenia, in a situation where there were concerns after events in 1988 that the sovereignty of the Republic was not being respected, then the parliament and authorities in the Republic of Slovenia, from a different perspective but, essentially, the same activity, sought to strengthen its sovereignty.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Am I right in understanding that the amendments you are talking about, as far as Serbia is concerned, were all related to the specific situation of smaller areas under the sovereignty, not under the sovereignty, but within the Republic of Serbia, the autonomous regions, it was just related to that internal Serbian matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is very difficult to answer because, although the two autonomous provinces were within Serbia and it was a question in Serbia for the integrity of the Serbian Republic as a whole, it was a matter of significance within the SFRY, because the two autonomous provinces were given representation; for example, the collective presidency were regarded as having certain status at the federal level. Therefore, the Republic of Serbia by taking these measures with regard to the political authority on territories within the Republic of Serbia were also taking actions which were having effect on the SFRY as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I can imagine that it would have effect, that it was not without effect to measures taken within the Republic of Serbia, but did Serbia in these amendments not accept the primacy of the federal constitution any more? Did it put its own constitution on a higher level than the federal constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure if it did or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: That was my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure if it did or not. I believe that it did not in a formal sense although, clearly, by the assertion of sovereignty it was doing so in a de facto sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, I am aware that it is a very complex matter, but my question was whether in this constitution the primacy of the federal constitution was put away and it was done away with. Was this the case in the Slovenian amendment? Did they say in their new constitution that whenever there would be a conflict in the constitutional provisions between the Federation and the Slovenian constitution that the Slovenian constitution would prevail?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that that is the case and that would be consistent with any state deciding on the exercise of its sovereign rights going back to the point that the republics were defined as sovereign entities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Gow, if I take you to another part of your testimony of yesterday and the day before yesterday: When the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised by some European states, could you define precisely for us the exact territory of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina that was recognised at that time? What was exactly the territory of the state, the status of territory, people, what was the territory, could you indicate it on one of the maps you used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Gladly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Your maps are made under your direction so you know them better which one is suitable for .....

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will probably use the first map. It is the most straightforward, I would have thought.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: This is Exhibit 2, would it be?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Exhibit 2. (Handed)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am afraid I have lost the pointed stick I was given the other day. I think, quite clearly, the borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina -- let us try again. After my difficulty in long distance manipulation of this thing yesterday, I had better be very careful. You will see here this line, if you follow it round, indicates the borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina. You will see that also the very tiny strip there of it which goes to the Adriatic Sea.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gow. Was there a central government in the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina at that moment of recognition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Where was it based?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Sarajevo. Did this government exercise all the I say usual state functions on the whole of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am afraid I am not sure what it is that you are asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I, perhaps, give you a better example.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: OK.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: For example, it is usually accepted that responsibility for the police working in your territory is one of the functions of a government. Was the central government of Sarajevo controlling the police on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there is a different between responsibility and control. Governments have responsibility even if they do not always have control of situations. I know in my own country and in the United States sometimes there are areas in which -- no doubt in other countries -- Police Forces act in inappropriate ways. But I do not think that removes the responsibility of the government for what is taking place because governments are charged with the responsibility even if they are not actually able to control things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: When I am talking about control, I am not meaning to say that sometimes a police officer might do something that is not correct and it should have prevented him to do so, but I am talking about where there was in general terms. Let us just give an example, was the Sarajevo government controlling the Prijedor police, for example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Controlling, as far as I can talk about the Prijedor Police Force, I am not sure that it was, I am not sure that it was, but again I do not think that removes its responsibility as the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is difficult situation like so many of the others which we are discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you have already two times drawn my attention to a formal responsibility. Is this a way of expressing that it really was a formal responsibility instead of giving directions to them, orders being obeyed, so that is what I understand when I am talking about control of the Police Forces, and not a formal responsibility that, in effect, does not mean anything. Could you please clarify the position in existence at the time of the recognition of this state, as far as -- I am just taking this example -- the Police Forces are concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no specific knowledge of the situation in a comprehensive and absolute sense with regard to the Police Force in any individual part of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Having made that clear as a reservation, I would not be surprised at all in the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1990 and '91, or indeed into the beginning of 1992, to find that there were some areas where there were policemen who might receive instructions from Sarajevo but would not act on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Let me then talk about another essential state function, the monetary aspects. For example, at that time in western Herzegovina was there a situation where Croats had their own currency and, perhaps, also their own police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe you could clarify the question again? I am sorry to keep doing this but it is .....

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I am trying to find out about the effective functioning of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time of the recognition.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: OK.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I start asking about whether they were in control of the police. You said: "Well, I do not know; it might be that they were not in certain areas". Another essential state function is controlling the monetary institutions and currency. Were there areas in Bosnia-Herzegovina, for example, in western Herzegovina, where Croats were having their own currency instead of using the official currency of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the Croats in the area you identified were not using their own currency.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: They were not using their own currency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were using -- but the currency the Republic of Croatia was freely circulating, and this is rather like going to Luxembourg and being able to use Belgium francs, I guess. If you regard the territory of the SFRY before its dissolution, Deutschemark was the most used currency, I would guess, for most transactions apart from grocery shopping and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Is that not an indication that the currency of the country involved does not function properly ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure if it is an indication.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: -- from a monetary point of view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure if it is an indication that the currency of the country does not function properly any more than the free use of the Belgium franc in Luxembourg indicates that Luxembourg does not function as a country, or that the free use of the Deutschemark, or relatively free use of the Deutschemark, in the territories of the SFRY before its dissolution indicated that the financial currency systems there did not work. I would also express the judgment in the case of the SFRY they did not, but I am not sure that it makes the point clearly one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps another state function, taxes. Were taxes collected all over the territory by the central government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the situation in 1991 and 1992, I very much doubt it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: You doubt it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I doubt it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: What about another state function, Defence, army; could you tell us about the army of the central government of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I assume that you are still talking at the time of the recognition of independent international personality of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and if that is the case -----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I am talking about this period, then we might move to another period later.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just for clarification, yes. At the time of the recognition of independent international personality of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as with so many other things again, there was a complex situation. The government of Bosnia and Herzegovina had responsibility for the Territorial Defence forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina. At the same time, I have already discussed the presence of the Yugoslav People's Army on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I think I have indicated that there were a presence of a number of irregular armed groups on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that there was the presence of the Croatian army on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I hope that that addresses the question, but again I may be not clear about what it is that you are asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: What was the control of the Sarajevo government and the control used in the same sense as I explained before of the armed forces on the territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The government of Bosnia and Herzegovina had control of the central elements of the Territorial Defence and of Territorial Defence in other areas. In some areas, I already gave evidence that there had been activity to move, to change the complexion of the Territorial Defence Force and to mobilize ethnic Serbs into certain Territorial Defence units in preparation for possible action at a later stage. In the case of those units, although the central Territorial Defence command might well have been issuing them instructions still, I am quite sure that if they were getting instructions they were paying no attention to those instructions. With regard to the Yugoslav People's Army, the situation at this time remained a little bit ambiguous because the JNA had been going through this process of transformation, and elements within it were clearly orientated to and in knowledge of plans for actions that would come later. There was still a strong Yugoslav sense in elements of the JNA. Some of these people in Sarajevo were talking to the Bosnian government, were seeking to try, perhaps even more than the Bosnian government might have been, to resolve the situation, to try to prevent a further deterioration. With regard to the situation, I mentioned the presence of the Croatian army, at this stage, although the Croatian army was present, my recollection is that it was formally being indicated as being present to give support to the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, although the nature of its presence was later certainly not to be of that nature, and with regard to control of the various irregular types of force, apart from Territorial Defence forces, maybe called irregular in some uses of terminology, with regard to control of those other irregular forces, I would say that the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina almost certainly had no control whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please be a bit more precise on which parts of the Territorial Defence, because you said that some might have been under the control of the central government and some parts not, was this according to the spreading of the ethnic community, so to say that where there was a majority of Serbs there was no control of this Territorial Defence there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would regard it as being reasonable, to use the word again, to suppose that in Serbian majority, certainly in a number of areas with a Serbian majority population as well as in some more mixed areas, in accordance with evidence that I already gave and in accordance with some of the documentation that I gave, that in some of those areas those, indeed, were areas in which the instructions of the Territorial Defence command of Bosnia and Herzegovina would be ignored or not received.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: If you are talking about those areas, could you say approximately what percentage of the country that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure that I could say approximately what percentage. I would say -- no, I do not think I could give an approximate percentage.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gow. I do not know whether -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Before you go to your next question, Mr. Orie, we will stand in recess for 20 minutes. (11.30 a.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Orie, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: If I may proceed, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, first go back to a few items we discussed this morning and then with some constitutional issues. First, going back to the question of Slovenes or Serbians being not loyal any more to the federative constitution, would it be fair to say that the Slovenes were the first to give up on Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I am really not quite sure what the question is asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: My question is whether it is fair to say that the Slovenes were the first to give up on Yugoslavia? It is a short question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a short question. I am just not sure.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think he asked what you mean. He does not understand what you mean by "give up". Is that the problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: What would you understand -- how would you understand it, if I may ask that question to you so I know where is the uncertainty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not ----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: If you say it does not mean anything at all, that is also an answer to me and I could try to rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that case, I am not sure if I am allowed to talk?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: My question was, if you say this question makes no sense and for that reason I cannot answer it, I would be glad to hear, but my question was whether it would be fair to say that the Slovenes were the first to give up on Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you understand the question, Dr. Gow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure that I do.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Would you rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: OK. Perhaps I put another question to you. What did you mean when you said to the Committee of Foreign Affairs of the House of Commons that the Slovenes were the first to give up on Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that case, yes. In that context what I meant was that, although I do not recall using those exact words, but in that context I was indicating that at the latest by the end of 1990 in spite of some, and here I am talking about the political authorities of the Republic of Slovenia, that Slovenes in that sense refers to the political authorities of the Republic of Slovenia, by the end of 1990 at the latest had decided that there was no future in the SFRY and had begun making preparations for the independence of Slovenia. I am glad that you put it in this way because it is easier to conceptualize and it takes away the word "fair" which gave me some difficulty. I hope I have answered adequately.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I come back to another area we touched upon this morning and that is the protection of Serbs in Croatia. I asked about their position under the constitution, the downgrading, and we talked about legislation on citizenship. You said, well, I did not know anything about that. Do you know of any other specific legislation concerning the position of the Serbians in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Specific legislation concerning?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, grounds and rights. We saw them being downgraded as not being mentioned any more as the next to the Croats as the ones to whom belonged the state of Croatia. Is there any perhaps not legislation on citizenship, not a constitution, but any other legislation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Do you think that any protection in legal terms would have been effective as far as Serbs in Croatia were concerned? Could they really expect the laws to be respected as far as they were concerned by the state and anyone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would have thought as far as anybody else could.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: You mean there was no rule of law in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would mean that in the situation of transition I would not count on any anything being completely effective in any part of the territories of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: But there are no specific questions, no specific concerns as far as the position of the Serbs in Croatia were concerned? I mean, you are now describing a general situation where no one was sure whether the rule of law would be applied or not, but specific concerns for Serbs in that area prior to the independence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I have understood correctly, and you are asking me if Serbs in Croatia expressed concerns, then it is the case that Serbs in Croatia expressed concerns.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: No, that was not my question. My question was whether there was any real concern perhaps in your opinion for the effective protection of Serbs in the Croatian republic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, again if I have understood correctly, you are asking me if in my judgment the concern expressed by the Serbs was justified and, if I have understood that correctly, then I take you back to an answer I gave before, which is that it was the case that given the historical experience Serbs in the area might have some concern in this situation. Whether or not that concern would justify actions that were taken, including the erection of barricades, the arming of populations, whether the concerns extended as far as a level where it would be necessary to take those measures, I am by no means entirely clear that that was case, which is not to say that in local areas there were incidents which would inevitably give cause for concern. Equally, there were incidents against ethnic Croats in Croatia in this period, again where the Croatian government was not able effectively to enforce whatever kind of responsibilities or protections it might be expected to carry out. It is a very difficult question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: So you would not question specifically the activity of the protection under the rule of law of the Serbs in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would think that it comes into question certainly to the extent that in some areas of Croatia where there were Serbian majority populations local Serbian officials, with perhaps support from elsewhere, effectively created a type of control over those territories, so the effective protection of Croatian law, of the Croatian authorities was de facto not possible irrespective of any other consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Do you think, Dr. Gow, that any legal provision protecting Serbs in Croatia would be meant to be serious?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure that it is a question I can really give an answer to. It involves a degree of speculation which I do not think would be appropriate. Maybe I have missed the nature of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: What I asked, and that is what I started with as a matter of fact, to find out whether in your eyes specific concern about the legal protection of Serbs in the Republic of Croatia was justified or not, whether it is your opinion that there should be concern about their protection under the rule of law, seriousness, activity of the protection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This really is very complex and difficult. I indicated that because local Serbians had taken effective control of certain areas, to discuss it in terms of the effective implementation of the rule of law by the Zagreb authorities seems to be almost a question but almost a non-question. I would judge that the Zagreb authorities would be charged with responsibility for that situation, but whether or not, but in a situation where de facto Croatian police force were not able to go into areas, it seems difficult to talk about the Croatian government whether or not the legal provisions -- maybe before I finish this could I ask you it repeat the question to make sure I am still answering it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Well, my first question ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, if you do not mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I started asking you whether there were any legal statutes specifically protecting or at least mentioning Serbs to be protected in the Croatian republic. That is what I started with. The answer was that you do not know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: You do not know. Then a more general second question was whether, so not under a specific Statute, but whether the Serbs could expect that a rule of law would be applied as far as those were concerned as well, so that is to say that the protection of the law would be effective for them as well and that the protection given by law to them would be meant to be a serious protection by those who legislated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If that is your question, then the Serbs in those areas presumably would not expect the Croatian authorities, effectively, to implement the rule of law because, de facto, Serbs in the area had taken control of those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you whether these words sound familiar to you: "Prior to the declaration of independence there was a legal Statute which specifically mentioned the Serbs and offered certain kinds of protections and guarantees. Protections were there legally. The question would have been whether they could have been enforced; whether or not they were serious or whether they were like under the Communist constitutions a mere formality." Is that a fair description of the situation as far as the protection of Serbs is concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not a judgment with which I would disagree.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: You would not disagree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
