utterances.text: Does this mean that you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I mean I would -- I use that terminology to convey again that it is a complex situation, but I certainly would not disagree with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: My first question was whether these words were familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As such they are not familiar, but it is not impossible even that I might have written them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, or have expressed them in the House of Commons. Dr. Gow, I was not able to phrase the question properly this morning and I give it a new try, if you do not mind. Could a republic legitimately succeed to form a new nation state from its majority population under the 1974 constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, I am not absolutely clear what it is that you are asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I did not understand you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, but again I am not exactly clear what it is that you are asking me. I understand all the words but I am not quite clear what exactly it is you are asking me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Could a republic legitimately secede to form a new nation state for its majority population under the 1974 constitution? I am quite willing to repeat it again for you. I must say I got some help from my learned English friends in rephrasing the question, so I am a bit less uncertain about the language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Would it not speed matters up if you said what you thought he meant and see if he agrees? It is not much good just keeping on repeating the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I agree and if that is agreeable I can try.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is a distinction that I would make between legality and legitimacy and I am not sure what the precise answer would be in either case. The answer to the question would be a compound of the interpretation of legal factors, political factors and I would guess also international factors. Legality would, as far as I understand it from a political perspective, derive from various levels, or could possibly derive from various levels of constitutional law and related aspects of law and from elements of public international law, and that is one factor which played a role in the dissolution of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. I state that not as a matter of my own interpretation; simply as a matter of record. This is something, a fact which occurred on the basis of those elements. In terms of legitimacy which would for me would imply a series of other possibilities which might be ethical, they might be socio-politically constitutive and supportive; they might be based on a series of other factors. If you wish me to go into some kind of an effort to describe things in terms of that kind of political terminology, I would do so, but if I have answered your question already then I would be happy to stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, I would rather have you to answer my question. If you say these are two answers. First, could a republic legally secede to, and the second question, could a republic legitimately secede, I would like to know your opinion. I am quite well aware that you must have good reasons for taking that opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the first of your questions, the legal aspects of secession are difficult and were the subject, I say this again, as a matter of fact, a matter that is record, was something that was being argued about on the territories of the SFRY in the latter period of the SFRY. It involved arguments about a complex set of interpretations of provisions of the constitution, some of the provisions you asked me about earlier this morning, some provisions I made reference to to indicate these discussions in earlier parts of my testimony. The legal right to secession was applied to the peoples. Sovereignty was given to the republics. The interpretation of sovereignty which was, as far as I understand it, current on the territories of the SFRY in its latter period was in the sense of sovereignty, meaning in the end the right not to be subject to interference from outside, and that in a formal sense under the communist constitutions which I stressed before originally were intended not to have real meaning, that quality of sovereignty or some elements of the quality of sovereignty, some of the sovereign rights, were exercised through the federation, rather in the same way that the Member States of the European Union exercise some of their sovereign rights through the formation of the Union. Here let me be clear, I am not saying that SFRY was the European Union; simply to illustrate the nature of this exercise of sovereign rights as a matter of principle. The Member States of the European Union have clearly indicated as a matter of proper political will that this is what they want to do. In the case of the communist constitutions of the SFRY and the Federal People's Republic, it was more a formal connotation, but to be clear, in principle, as a matter of technicality, it was the same kind of transfer. Therefore, if sovereignty was the ultimate right to decide on matters within a territory, and that inhered with the republics. In the conventional sense of the application of the right to self-determination, the use of the term "people" applies to those inhabiting a territory, a pre-designated political community with territorial boundaries and perhaps certain other qualities, then rather than an ethno-national grouping wherever it might be found, then an argument was made and could be made and was accepted as a matter of fact in the dissolution of Yugoslavia by the International Community that that was the case. In the context of the SFRY constitution, to come back precisely to answering your question, and you will see from what I have said so far it is a complex and difficult question ----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I have become aware of that, Dr. Gow!

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That in the nature of the discussions it was understood that the republics were sovereign states, the discussion in both Serbia and in Slovenia was on the nature of the sovereignty of those states within the SFRY, and in the case of Slovenia in the latter stages outside the SFRY. The question about the exercise of sovereign rights coming to the legal right to secession, if you are talking about the right to secession, then that would be applied to the peoples. The ambiguity of the preamble of the introductory part of the constitution would indicate that you could try to interpret that use of "peoples" of "narod" in two ways. I indicated in the first two lines it is used in two different senses, although in Serbo-Croat it is one word. In that context there could be an argument about whether or not the right to secession inhered with the ethno-national group of the first line or with the peoples implicitly of a territory of the second line. I think it was clearly understood from the nature of the one of the extracts we played yesterday on the video monitor, President Milosevic in 1990 was proposing that there should be a formal change to the constitutional structure of the SFRY in his discussions with the Slovenian President to move, to make it an equal right of all ethno-national groups rather than being one of territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And so, the end of this long, complex answer is, it would depend, in part it might depend on your perspective whether or not there was a legal right, that the legal right, if there was a legal right it was a sum of factors, and as a political fact that right was not necessarily a factor in the final dissolution of the SFRY, because in the eyes of the majority of the states of the SFRY in the international community the final breakup of the SFRY was regard as a matter of the non-functioning of the federation and dissolution rather than a matter of secession anyway. But in answer to your question, legally it depended on your perspective and it would depend on the constitution -- the wrong word -- on the compound of factors involved in the particular situation and the interpretations applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, am I right in understanding that you find it a complex question on which you have no clear opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I actually thought the complexity, that I had expressed a clear opinion. If I have not, then forgive me and I would be happy to try to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: If I may express myself, I heard so many if's and if you would look at it this way and that way, that I think the words of Shakespeare came into my mind: If if's and and's were pots and pans there would be no need of tinkers!

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which means?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, let me see if I can understand you. Are you saying, yes, the 1974 constitution would allow secession if you defined "nation" in the first line, I think it is the first line, perhaps it is the second, I think it is the first line of the 1974 constitution, to constitute a republic as opposed to a group of peoples? Can you just answer that and try to make it as short as possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reference to peoples of a territory is in the second line and on the basis of sovereignty expressed in the constitution and in the constitutions of the republics with appropriate agreement expressed under Article 5 of the SFRY constitution, then it would be legal.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The legality of it would be dependent on agreement in terms of Article 5.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. Does that help? Yes, if you define the word "nation" in the first line in a certain way. Then you went on to say, well, I will not go into what Milosevic said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Having no clear opinion because it depends on how you present it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think he is giving you an answer. Yes, if you define "nation" in a certain way, but then you have to look at Article 5 of the constitution. Then he said, well, Milosevic took a certain position and I do not know what effect that would have on the legal definition. Finally, he says it does make any difference anyway because the dissolution was not because of anything that was written in the 1974 constitution. That is how I hear his answer. But, in answer to your first question, it appears, yes, if you define "nation" in a certain way. Is that correct, Dr. Gow, or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That seems correct to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to think over during the lunch break whether I would like to have replayed the Milosevic tape on this.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. I do not mean to interfere, but I was trying to see if we could get closure on that one point. MR. ORIE (To the witness): Dr. Gow, I would like to touch upon a few other constitutional issues, but I now turn to Bosnia-Herzegovina. In your testimony on May 9th, you said that the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina affirmed the sovereignty of the republic as we have seen it in Exhibit 47. You have also noted that most of the Serbian representatives did not participate in that vote. Am I correct in stating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know, Dr. Gow, whether the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina in force at that time had a requirement of proportional representation of the nations and nationalities of Bosnia-Herzegovina in parliament?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of the precise details of the arrangements in Bosnia and Herzegovina, but I can say that as with elements of the SFRY as a whole, in some areas there was a principle of ethno-national proportionality. In the SFRY as a whole, there were two chambers, one like some kind of direct election and the other to be based on a kind of proportional proportionality. I believe that was also the case in Bosnia and Herzegovina. In the case of presidency, the collective presidency, of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there was a formal provision that two representatives would be served, two would be Croat, two would be Muslim and one would be designated -- would be a self-defining Yugoslav.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: That would reflect the same idea?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know whether the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina in force at that time contained any special mechanism for deciding any question said to violate the principle of equality of the nations and nationalities of Bosnia-Herzegovina and so on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is my understanding that the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the 1974 constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, identified the three principal groupings, the Slav Muslims, the Croats and the Serbs, as the constituent peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I believe that there was an amendment to the constitution in 1990, the precise detail of which I cannot give to you, but the effect of which was to indicate that there would be some degree of protection for the interests of ethno-national communities in making significant changes within Bosnia and Herzegovina, the constitutional order in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know whether the special procedure you were just referring to as an amendment of 1990 in the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina for deciding such sensitive questions was followed in regard of October 16th adoption of the platform, the platform as we have seen it in Exhibits 47?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know if it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: You do not know whether it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I thought your question was, was this procedure followed and my answer was I do not know if it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In this platform, paragraph 2 of numbered clause 1, it says, "Any possibility of outvoting in the process of decision making on crucial issues concerning the equal rights of all nations and nationalities living in the Republic will be precluded through an appropriate structure of the Assembly of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina". Would it be correct to say that the purported adoption of this platform was such a case of outvoting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Would it be possible to look at the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Exhibit 47. (Handed)?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you mind repeating the question now?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I will repeat my question. Since it is written down, it is easy for me repeat it even literally. Paragraph 1 of numbered clause 1 of the platform, that is Exhibit 47 says, "Any possibility of outvoting in the process of decision making on crucial issues concerning the equal rights of all nations and nationalities living in the republic will be precluded through an appropriate structure of the Assembly of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina". My question was, would it be correct to say that the purported adoption of this platform was a case of such outvoting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it would not be the case because the Serbian representatives were not in the parliament at the time. Had Serbian representatives been in the parliament and voted against it, then it would be a question of outvoting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, in your testimony on the morning of May 9th, you stated that when the European Community invited republics of Yugoslavia to apply for recognition that the presidency and government of Bosnia and Herzegovina did so. Did the decision of those bodies, I am talking about the presidency and the government, include participation by the Serb members elected in the free elections of 1990, just 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The decision did not involve participation of those members elected in 1990. It involved -- because, as I indicated yesterday, Mrs. Plavsic and Mr. Koljevic had left the presidency -- I am sorry, can you tell me which period you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I am talking about the moment that the EC invited republics of Yugoslavia to apply for recognition and then you said the presidency and government of Bosnia and Herzegovina did so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the question is? Did the Serbian representatives participate in the decision? I do not know if they participated in the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have a thing that was not quite clear to me and, since we are talking about members of the presidency and the government of the Bosnia-Herzegovina, I would like to have this specific part of the tape we saw yesterday replayed where Arkan meets, as far as I remember, a lady. I would like to see that again. I do not know exactly, I lost a bit, but perhaps the Prosecution could help me?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 69 is the Exhibit we did not hear from -----

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: 69, part 2.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is it part 2?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Part 2, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The first 69, part 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I am not that much interested in the first part, but a meeting with a lady on the street, if that is clear enough.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is in the first frame, I think, 13.34. Is that true, Mr. Niemann, do you know? , anyway you want us to play 69?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Part 2. Can you locate that quickly?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: This part. (Video extract was played)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You want to stop? You want it to go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. (To the witness): I would like to ask you a question on this, on the specific part of the video. You testified, you gave the name of the lady -- I think she was a member of the Bosnia-Herzegovina presidency -- could you please repeat that so we know who it is, the lady?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Biljana Plavsic who was a member -- a Serbian representative to the collective presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: That is the same person you referred to one or two minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was beginning to answer the long question, when I realised the time frame was different, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You testified that she is congratulating Arkan for his success. Could you please tell us what is the source of this knowledge, because I did not hear any sound on the specific video tape part? My question was, how do you know that she is congratulating Arkan because that is what you testified yesterday with his military success. You gave an interpretation of what she said to him, but I would like you to tell us the source of this knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The source of knowledge I express, I make that statement on the basis of the reports of people who, reports made at the time in newspapers and reports made to researchers involved in the making of this film who were going there and finding the excerpts of the film. Mrs. Plavsic was there as part of a Bosnia and Herzegovina presidency delegation which involved the Bosnian Defence Minister, a Croat, Jelko Doko, and a couple of other people, I forget the names exactly. But Mrs. Plavsic, who went to investigate the incidents and, as I understand it, Mrs. Plavsic went away from the other groups and met with Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that she has a meeting with Arkan, I think, is quite clear. Could you be a bit more precise because you told us that she congratulated him with his success. You said: "Well, I heard this from sources". I wonder whether these sources are on this video screen because there are just a few people -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you want it there?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you want it to stay on there?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: So perhaps we could see who is within hearing distance. Is there any of these people on the screen that is one of your sources?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not believe so, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Could you now be more precise in your source? You refer to sources within a rather general way. Could you please tell me exactly who came to this conclusion and on what basis and at what time this was told to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I indicated that my recollection is that at the time there were newspaper reports and that Mrs. Plavsic had made expressions. That is my recollection. That is supplemented, and the central part of my making this statement is based on the researchers involved in making this programme who went to the region, who obtained the film and who talked to people who were there and who had been in the area and who had been involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Again you are not giving specific names of people who said, "I heard this", more or less?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The researcher on The Cook Report programme is Paul Calverley.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from that, you say you saw this in newspaper articles? This is also a source you are basing your opinion on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My recollection is that there was reporting of the incident in Bijeljina at the time, and my recollection is that Mrs. Plavsic and what I described as congratulating Arkan -- and I think the greeting and the kiss itself is an indication of that; it might not be but I would say that it is a fair interpretation of that moment -- and the meeting of Mrs. Plavsic and Arkan was reported and reported in a way which indicated that Mrs. Plavsic was, indeed, congratulating Arkan. If the reports were not accurately founded, I cannot say, but the reports there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Is that what you meant to say yesterday, that she was congratulating Arkan, if the sources you used are reliable and if they are not reliable she was not congratulating Arkan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I would judge the sources to be reliable and, therefore, I would return to the original statement which is my judgment is that she was, indeed, congratulating Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: One of your sources you just mentioned were newspapers articles, could you tell us what newspapers? That is Serbian newspapers, were they Muslim newspapers, were they Croatian newspapers, were they Western newspapers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no recollection now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: You have no recollection? One of the other -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was reading a variety of newspapers at the time. I could not say that it appeared in any particular one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I would also indicate that the same interpretation has appeared in a number of other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: You also indicated, did I understand you well, Dr. Gow, the way, how she was greeting him was an indication that she congratulated him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is my interpretation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gow, for this part. I will continue with the constitutional aspects of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We did talk about whether there was any outvoting or not. We did talk about the participation of Serb members of the Bosnian parliament and presidency -- I am sorry, I have to find the place where I stopped. Yes, I think my last question before drawing your attention to this Arkan tape was whether the elected Serbian members of the Bosnian presidency -- no. If you give me just two seconds to find the place where I was. Yes, my next question to you, Dr. Gow, is did the elected Serbian members of the Bosnian presidency give a reason for their boycott of their body's activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not -- I do not recall if they gave a specific explanation, but I can give, as far as I recall, a broad not a specific explanation, but what I think my recollection is, the general explanation for that boycott.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: General explanation. I will ask you whether the elected Serbian members gave a reason, so you say: "I am not aware of any reason given by these elected members"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I indicated that I could not give the specific reason given because I do not recall a specific reason being given, but I can indicate the general reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: General reason given by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the part of the Serbian representatives to whom you made reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: OK. I do understand that you are not giving the reasons explicitly mentioned by the elected members, but a general understanding of what their reason was; is that what you would like to tell us? I would like you to do that, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall the text or precise content of any specific statement. The context for this had been, I think, four or five days of discussion on the sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina, much of which, I believe, was behind closed doors, and was also following from an earlier discussion on the same question in February of the same year. In both cases, the Serbian population -- the Serbian or at least a majority, I do not know if all, Serbian representatives had formed the position that they opposed this action, and that the non-participation in the parliamentary session to which I think you were making reference was because of a general sense that they did not want to be party to a decision of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Was part of this general understanding of the reasons also that a decision of this kind was an unconstitutional decision? They did not want to participate in the decision "of this kind", you said, without specifying what a kind of decision this was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I thought -- perhaps I had misunderstood -- you had specified it was the decision on the statement, the platform on the sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina. If I was wrong on that, then perhaps you could correct me because I have been talking about the wrong thing completely for the last couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: No, I do not think there is a misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: OK, fine. In that case then -- I do not think, if I have remembered your question correctly now as being were the Serbian representatives not participating because they regarded the decision as unconstitutional, the narrow and specific answer is that I do not know if that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I am not asking whether it was the case or not. I started asking what was the reason given by the elected members. You said you could not answer that question, then you said: "But I can give you a general idea of what reason was regarded to be there not to participate any more".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: The last part of my question, where you said they refused to participate in these kinds of decisions, then my question was whether in this understanding of the reasons this was an unconstitutional position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think I am able to answer that question. I am not clear that I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I will ask my learned English friends to help me a bit to see whether my language is not clear enough. My next question to you, Dr. Gow is did the elected Serbian members of Bosnian presidency indicate the conditions under which they would again participate in the activities of that party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My recollection is that they did, but I do not have a specific recollection of what those conditions were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: You say no specific recollection, this means that -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is said my recollection is that they did, but I have no recollection of what the specific conditions were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, OK. Dr. Gow, did the elected Serb members of the Bosnian parliament and presidency after walking out of those bodies refuse to negotiate with the other political parties in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: That is a clear answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes -- no, there were negotiations so they must not have refused -- I do not know if they made a declaration of refusal or not, but they took part in some negotiations at later stages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: The answer was quite clear to me, Dr. Gow, the answer was no. You referred in your testimony on May 9th to the constitution of the Serbian Republic of Bosnian and Herzegovina of 28th February 1992 as a provisional constitution. Did that constitution, provisional constitution, contain provisions indicating a willingness to negotiate continuing ties with other peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Article 4 of that constitution indicated the possibility of forming, of establishing, links with I think units, I do not remember precisely, of other communities in Bosnia and Herzegovina but, as I would read it, was dependent on Article 3 which indicated that the declared Serbian Republic would remain part of Federal Yugoslavia. So, in a sense ---

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: It was not an explicit provision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- in a sense Article 4 could be saying, if there was a willingness to join in this new mini Yugoslavia by other peoples, then that would be a possibility which was open.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: It had to be negotiated in one way or the other. Thank you, Dr. Gow. You noted several times that the constitution of the Serbian Republic in Bosnia and Herzegovina says that the Republic is a part of the Federal Yugoslavia, that is Article 3 you just mentioned. Did federal Yugoslavia, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, ever recognise this claim of membership by the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The authorities of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia did not formally at any stages, as far as I am aware, recognise the incorporation of that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: So they did not ever recognise this claim of membership of the Bosnian Serbs? That is how I understand your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in a formal legal sense, but as the argument was made at certain stages in the dissolution of Yugoslavia on the right of those Serbs or of people in those areas or wherever it was to remain united in a common state of the Serb people, as General Kadijevic put it in his book, then again it is another, yet another, complex, ambiguous situation. There was no formal legal recognition, but there was quite clearly pursuance of the question in political dimensions and in the context of the writings of General Kadijevic in the military political dimension as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a clear answer and I see that it is complex again. I would like you to refer to Exhibit 52. (Handed) You have Exhibit 52? It is decision No. 4 of the Badinter Committee. If you look at page 3, as you have noted on May 9th, the Badinter acknowledged that the fact that the activities of Serb officials and the result of a plebiscite of Serbs created the circumstances under which the will of the peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina to constitute a republic as a sovereign and independent state could not be held to have been fully established, and Mr. Badinter also said that a referendum was possibly a means for indicating this. You have noted that such a referendum was held. Was the decision to hold the referendum supported by the elected Serbian officials in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not supported by members of the Serbian Democratic Party. There were some Serbs who were elected who were still part of the parliament and who, I believe, were supporting this. So if you mean the representative of the Serbian Democratic Party, then the answer is that they did not, I think, if that was the question -----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: How much Serbian representatives were there who were a member of that Party and how many Serbian representatives were there that were not a member of the Party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember how many in either case, but the overwhelming majority of Serbian representatives in the Assembly were from the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: You have noted that many Serbs did not vote in this referendum. Do you remember what the percentage of Serbs was in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The percentage was approximately 31 per cent, maybe a little more, broadly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: A little over 30?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A little over 30 per cent, around a third of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: What was the percentage of the people that voted, how many per cent voted, in this referendum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My recollection was that it was 63 and a half per cent, something again, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Under these circumstances, is it possible that a referendum could be said to establish the will of the peoples -- I emphasise that I am using the plural, just as Mr. Badinter does -- of Bosnia and Herzegovina to constitute it as an independent state? Was this a decision of the peoples?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure what a decision of the peoples exactly would be, but it was certainly taken by Monsieur Badinter and the European Council of the European Communities as being such.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you would allow me, we have had a difficult time in preparing this cross-examination, because one of the members of our team was not present. If you would not mind to stop now, five minutes early, and I would like to bring to your attention that the Prosecution, although we really try to work hard, had some difficulties in mastering all the complex problems that have been touched upon by Mr. Gow. We would like to use our lunch break to discuss whether it will be possible for us to continue all afternoon. I am telling you why, because we need a bit of time and the weekend is almost there. So, I am not saying that we cannot finish this afternoon. We will certainly continue after the lunch break. But, as Article 21 of the Statute says, we are entitled to have not only facilities for our defence but time as well. You will understand that this is an expert witness. We will not repeat this with every witness of fact, but I would like to indicate that we will discuss it over lunch and we will then see how far we come this afternoon and we might ask you -- perhaps you can consider it already -- that if we would like to stop at, let us say, 3 o'clock or at 4 o'clock, and ask you to adjourn until next Monday so that we continue, then at least we have some 48 extra hours time to think of all the very complex problems that are contained in the statement of Dr. Gow.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You will be ready to proceed after our lunch recess? At 2.30 you will be ready to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but we do not know whether we will be ready to finish it.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So you perhaps will want additional time, that we adjourn early and that you continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: That we continue on Monday because it is not just a matter of time, but also we need libraries, we need sources, to consult, etc. That is the reason why we might ask you this afternoon to adjourn a bit earlier and continue on Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I just had one question, Dr. Gow, on this point and I am trying to understand your testimony of yesterday, Dr. Gow. 63 per cent of the entire population of Bosnia and Herzegovina voted, was that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of the entire electorate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Of the entire electorate, entire, I gather, persons who were registered; I have no knowledge of whether there was a registration requirement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: 63 per cent of elected persons voted. You said just a few minutes ago that approximately 31 per cent of the population at that time in Bosnia-Herzegovina were Serbian. Do you know what percentage of the Serbian electorate boycotted the election? Did you tell us that yesterday or whenever it was you testified about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not tell you that. I do not think I am in a position to tell you that. I would be surprised if anybody was in a position precisely to tell you that. All I can say is that a very large part, the overwhelming majority of the Serbian population boycotted the election, but there were Serbs in some areas who took part in it. Similarly, of course, some Muslims and Croats did not take part in it, I would guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know what per cent of the electorate were Serbians, the 31 per cent in Bosnia-Herzegovina, I gather, is 31 per cent of the entire population or was that 31 per cent of electorate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 31 per cent is of the entire population. I do not know what the precise share of the electorate was, but I see no reason to suppose that it was radically different.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Radically different, higher than other -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I see no reason to suppose that it was radically different, therefore, it would be broadly the same, would be my judgment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. We will stand in recess until 2.30. (1.00 p.m.) (Luncheon Adjournment (2.30 p.m.) PRIVATE

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Orie, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I am ready to proceed, your Honour. (To the witness): Dr. Gow, I would like to return very briefly to the question of the protection of Serbs in Croatia. Would it be correct to say that the 1991 census showed approximately 570,000 Serbs in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know if that would be correct. I do not know if that would be correct, but my understanding is that as a percentage of the population of Croatia the Serbians formed around 12 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: 12 per cent of the total population of how many?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A total population of around 4 and a half million, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: So 12 per cent would be make approximately 500,000, that is 12 per cent of 4 and a half million?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your arithmetic is obviously faster than mine again, but I am prepared to accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know approximately how many Serbs remain in Croatia by now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very approximately, yes, and the proportion would be less than five per cent -- I am sorry, would be less than, or be careful now, I am not sure what the figure I have in my mind is, whether it is five per cent or five per cent of those who were there before. But, an easier way of putting it is that more than 150,000, I do not know exact numbers, but certainly more than a 150,000, probably more than 200,000, Serbs left the territory of Croatia in the course of the last year and others left before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: So that would mean, if I go back to my arithmetics, that there would be still left some 200,000 or 300,000 Serbs. Of course, we started with a figure of 500,000 being 12 per cent of 4.5 million, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not think it would mean that, because if I recall what I just said, it was that in the course of the last year, 150,000, perhaps 200,000, Serbs left the territory of Croatia, but others left before that. I could not give you an exact number for the figure, but it was very large.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: The Serbs remaining, would it be less than 100,000 on Croatian territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say that is the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Less than 100,000 ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would be less than 100,000, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: -- at this moment. We talked this morning, Dr. Gow, on the protection of Serbs; we talked about the activity and the seriousness of the protection under the rule of law. In your answers you said that the Croatian government might not be able to, effectively, protect the Serbs in those areas where the Serbs themselves were in control. Were the Serbs living in Croatia mainly living in Serbian controlled areas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would answer the question with caution because of the term "mainly". About half the Serbian population, according to my recollection, my understanding, lived in those areas. Other parts of the Serbian population lived in other areas. There were significant Serb communities, for example, in the towns of Zagreb and Split and in other places. So maybe Serb, perhaps, approximately half, whether that constitutes slightly more than half or under half, I do not know exactly, lived in those Serb controlled areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: So there was a substantive number of Serbians living outside the Serbian controlled areas in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, are you aware of any reports of destruction of second homes of Serbs in the territory of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If by "reports" you mean generally of reports, then I am aware of the destruction or appropriation of second homes in Croatia, not just of Serbs, but as second homes of Serbs they would be included in the appropriation of second homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: What were the other homes that were either destroyed -- I am talking especially about destruction, not just about appropriation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure if destruction was involved, but there was a problem between the Republic of Slovenia and the Republic of Croatian regarding homes that were the property of Slovenian -- of citizens of the Republic of Slovenia; whether destruction was involved, I am not sure. It is not the kind of thing in which I found an enormous degree of interest, but that is my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: What time are we talking about when you are talking about reports of appropriation or destruction of homes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This would be in the period following the declarations of independence by Slovenia and Croatia -- whether or not it is a period which could be said to have finished, I am not sure -- but the period at least from the middle of 1991 until an unspecified, possibly not terminated -- for an unspecified and possibly not terminated period.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, are you aware of any reports of destruction of homes of Serbs in 1990, the summer of 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am aware that in the summer of 1990 there were incidents on the territory of the Republic of Croatia in which there was the use of -- there were attacks on the homes of citizens of the Republic of Croatia which were reported as being both of Serb origin and Croat origin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Where was that -- I was talking about second homes, summer houses, what area are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that case, if I may correct myself? I had forgotten that you were talking about second homes, and in the comment I just made it was simply with reference to attacks on homes; whether they were second homes or first homes, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: So, you are not aware of any specific reports on the destruction of Serbian second homes, summer houses, in the coastal areas in the summer of 1990?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of a specific report, if you have a specific report in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Doctor, I have not a specific report in mind. Are you aware of the fact that these were the first acts of destruction in the summer of 1990 against Serbian second homes, the first acts of destruction in the whole conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I cannot be aware of the acts to which you are making reference, I cannot be sure if they are the first acts, but as I am not aware anyway in a very complex situation exactly which was the first incident of violence, I do not think I can give a proper answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, I would like to take you to another subject. You testified extensively on the aims of the war, the aims of the Serbians, the aims to be achieved by the JNA on Croatian territory, and you made reference to a book which gave strong indications of what exactly these aims were. When you were talking about the different phases of attacking, different phases of the aims of the war in Croatia, is this a reconstruction based upon later publications like the publication of General -- I have forgotten his name, as a matter of fact ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kadijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: -- yes -- or was that clear from the beginning that that was the aim of that war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I am not clear what you are asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Was it clear already at the time when this war started, when this war was going on, was it already clear then what were the aims, or is your statement about what the aims were, or is it mainly based on what was later written on the subject, especially by the General you have just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, I would point out that the General in question was in charge of the Yugoslav People's Army at the time in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And it is not simply a matter of the General looking at a situation afterwards and providing an analysis of it. The General was involved and was at the heart of much of what was going on. In that case, I think it would be fair to say that, as far as the General describes certain situations and as far as the portion of evidence from General Panic would indicate as well, there was a clear idea in the JNA of what its objectives would be. So, therefore, they would have a clear idea; how precise and clear an idea at what stage would be difficult to say, but certainly that they had a clear idea, particularly in the latter stages about the borders of the designated areas that they were seeking to control, I think that is something which is clear by reference to the statements that they failed to accomplish their objectives in certain areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Kadijevic also indicated (and I believe I said this in testimony already) that it was necessary to operate under a certain rubric, that is -----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I could not understand your last answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, I think I already indicated that General Kadijevic suggested that it was necessary to operate under a certain rubric, that of separating the communities, in order to carry out what it regarded as its mission which was to assist the Serbian people, in this case, in Croatia. That in itself led to a situation in which, because there was no clearly defined, sorry, no clearly expressed objective on the part of the JNA, that in dealings with members of the International Community, for example, there continued to be a degree of uncertainty about some of what was actually going on, although many people in the area at the time, including the head of the European Community Monitor Mission, Henri Vijnaendts, indicated that they believed that there was an attempt to accomplish the kind of project to which I was making reference and which I think was indicated by General Kadijevic's book. Many people in Croatia and in other parts of Yugoslavia thought that it was clear what was going on. So my answer would be some people in parts of Yugoslavia thought it was clear what the JNA and Serbian military political forces were trying to achieve. It must have been clear to the JNA because we see that from the evidence of the Generals, but it was not always clear, because it was not explicitly expressed what the objectives were, to many outside observers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: My question was, Dr. Gow, whether it was clear to you; I know now whether it was clear to the JNA and quite many other people. Could you please express yourself whether it was clear at that time to you what the aims of the war were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think -- I take it that you are talking about the period of the war in Croatia in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And my judgment would be that in the period of 1991, not only after the declaration of independence of the Republic of Croatia on 25th June, but before that, there was evidence to suggest that elements of the JNA were co-operating with Serbian military political forces on the territory of the Republic of Croatia, but that in the transitional situation there were also parts of the Yugoslav People's Army which continued to hold to the idea of some version of Yugoslavia, and a version of Yugoslavia, of Tito's Yugoslavia, that they had in their minds. In this context, I think it is clear that although in the first part of 1991 there were some kind of discussions between representatives of the Serbian political leadership in Belgrade and the JNA -- some of which we saw reference made to in some of the tape clips played -- that there were differences of opinion during that period. So, it was not clear in part because some of what was being done was under a deliberate policy not to make it clear, and it was not clear and, therefore, was not clear to me in a way which I would regard as being absolutely conclusive; there were indications of collaboration in some areas but not indications at earlier stages. As far as I can recall, my judgment at the time, which is five years ago now and I am trying hard to remember how I saw things because my understanding evolves as more information comes to light, but at the time some aspects of war were not clear in particular because of the divisions of opinion and concerns of some within the JNA and the concerns of some people in some of the Yugoslav orientated people in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gow. You have spent part of your testimony on the ideology of a greater Serbia. Is this a unique ideology of the territory of the former Yugoslavia, that is to say, is this idea of a greater Serbia the only idealogy opposed to, let us say, the federal idealogy, or are there any other ideologies that would seek an expansion of their political power on the basis of ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, my memory is that I discussed not the idealogy of, although that is not necessarily an inappropriate term, but the idea of a great Serbia in the context of the 19th century, at which time I also indicated there was another idea, but that no doubt there were several ideas, but one idea to which I made reference was the Yugoslav idea, the Illyrian idea, that is, of a framework in which all the South Slavs would come together. That was the context in which I made reference to great Serbia. I am sorry. Could you repeat the last part of the question? I have forgotten it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: In answering, you said: "I mentioned, apart from the greater Serbia idea", whether you call it an idealogy or not is not of major importance at this moment, but you said, "I made reference also to another idea among several". Could you tell us what other ideas, apart from those you mentioned, you would think that existed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not say "among several". I said there may have been several, if my memory serves me correctly on that. No doubt there were any number of particular ideas. I would not in any sense regard myself as being an expert historian in this field in the 19th century, but I would not see that there would be any problem in supposing that there were some people who sought a state formation something for any of the particular communities that inhabited those territories and, in particular, certainly in the 20th century, there are many Croats who look to Middle Age Croatia and have that idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: So the greater Serbia idea is not unique to the extent that there is also a greater Croatian idea that goes already a bit back in history? Is this still vivid? Are you aware of any times when these ideas came up again? You are talking about the 20th century; is that just the whole century or specific times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, my memory of what I said was that there may have been an idea of a Croatian state. I see no reason -- I do not recall reading extensively about it, but I see no reason to suppose that this was not part of a framework of an intellectual discussion somewhere in the 19th century. When I made reference to the 20th century, I think the formation under the auspices of the Axes powers of the independent state of Croatia in the 1940s was an indication of what a type of great Croatian state might be because, as far as I understand it, the Medieval Kingdom of Croatia included parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and certain people believe that these should be part of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I have not seen much discussion of the fact that although the Bosnian Kingdom, when there was a Bosnian Kingdom, embraced large parts of Croatia and Serbia that Bosnia should take over those territories, but I do not exclude the possibility that somebody did say it some time, some place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: You are specifically referring to what happened in the 40s. Did this idea of a greater Croatia come back at a later stage of history?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The idea of a great Croatia is meaning one which is beyond the borders of the present Republic of Croatia. In territorial terms, you ask me in terms of the exercise of political power, I believe, but in territorial terms, there is certainly an idea which has been discussed in the 1990s, but that is an idea and an idea which, to some extent, some people may have sought to implement in the course of the 1990s on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, is there a similar idea, for example, as far as Macedonia is concerned? Are you aware of any developments there, a political attitude trying to achieve a greater Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of any significant movement in the 1990s attempting to achieve a greater Macedonia. I think that the Republic of Macedonia is constituted, has found itself in such a vulnerable and weak position that there has been in scope for serious and significant discussion of that kind. But again I do not exclude the possibility that there may be somebody or some people somewhere who may think in those terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Are you aware of the political party in Macedonia called IMRO, I-M-R-O?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I conventionally would refer to it VMRO, but, yes, the same, the internal Macedonian revolutionary organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Are you aware of greater Macedonian attitude in their political programme?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am aware that this organisation which was originally constituted at the end of the 19th century, I believe, with the assistance of Bulgarian authorities, I think, secret services, to be a terrorist organisation in the cause of seeking Macedonia as part of a great Bulgaria, and was significant, for example, in the assassination of King Alexander in Marseilles in 1934 -- I think I have made reference to that already -- was an outlaw organisation in the time of the Tito's Yugoslavia, reappeared as a political party in 1990, I think, with a more radical and a more moderate democratic wing clearly engaging in democratic politics and which might in some way have indicated an aspiration for a great Macedonia to incorporate parts of Bulgaria for union with Bulgaria. I am not aware that that was the case, but, equally, I would not by no means exclude the possibility that either in VMRO documents or in statements by members of the VMRO that they might have expressed aspiration of that kind, but I do not think that in terms of the situation in Macedonia that it is a question of any real significance.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: The IMRO party, could you give us an idea, is it an important party? For example, in the 1990 elections, what was their result? I mean, what was their achievement in the elections?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall either -- I do not recall their exact performance, but they, I think, were probably the largest single party elected and they certainly have formed part of a governing coalition.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Gow, on this subject. Dr. Gow, am I right in understanding that you testified that the non-Serbs (and I am really changing to a different subject) did little to prepare the war in '91 and '92 in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, could you repeat question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Is my understanding right that you testified that the non-Serbs did little to prepare for the war in '91 and '92 in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure if that is what I testified. I am prepared to believe that I might have said something broadly along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: So approximately it is what you -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall giving that testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: OK, if you would then please give your opinion on that, on how the non-Serbs prepared, whether or not little, for the war in '91 and '92 in a bit more detail?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yet again it is a question with no straightforward, simple answer. With regard to the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, by which I take it you would take to mean non-Serbs in this context, there were some limited efforts at fairly late stages to try to begin to develop the Territorial Defence as the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. At the same time at the political level until the very last moment, perhaps even beyond the very last moment, even into May 1992, the Bosnian presidency and government sought to achieve some kind of arrangement with the local command of the JNA to try to avert some of the conditions for the conflict which was either developing or by the later stages was underway. In the course of that, JNA and Bosnian government people co-operated in joint patrols to try to create calm and to try and secure the disarmament of certain non-formal groups, as far as that was possible. In doing so, to take a quote, an approximate quote, from a book written by Laura Silber, this was rather like putting the fox in charge of the chicken, a chicken coop. To some extent, that is true because parts of the JNA clearly were co-operating with elements of the Bosnian Serbs in preparing the way for the war. At the same time, I am prepared to believe that there were still some elements in the JNA who were seriously trying to co-operate, i.e. those who were not necessarily part of the kind of project, well, informed about the kind of project to which I made reference earlier. In the case of the Bosnian Croats, it was the case that in some areas in western Herzegovina, as the JNA had sought to disarm the Territorial Defence forces in very strongly Croat areas, the Territorial Defence forces, they had not accomplished that task and in some areas the local Croats had managed to keep control of some of the Territorial Defence weaponry. At the same time, elements of a group known as HOS, H-O-S, a Croatian paramilitary group which had been in Croatia in the time of the war there, had moved into western Herzegovina and it is possible to regard that as a preparation for conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Is this HOS group you are mentioning, was it a heavily armed group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The estimates for its size, I think, were around 15,000 and it was not heavily armed, if by that you mean weapons of heavy calibre which would be classified under the Conventional Forces in Europe Treaty, but it was certainly armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: You mentioned this HOS group, but that is, as far as I understand, a Croat paramilitary group. Were there any Muslim paramilitary groups active, preparing for what might come?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, yes, I was coming to mention -- there was a group called "Green Berets" which was a Muslim paramilitary group, the size of which is very hard. I have seen no reliable estimate of what the size of that group was. Certainly, it would have involved hundreds of people, quite probably might have involved thousands of people and, if I can anticipate the same kind of question, was not heavily armed but was armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: It was armed? Were they seeking more arms, Dr. Gow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know if they were seeking more arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please indicate whether the Green Berets was an organisation that was just a local organisation or was it spread over many places in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I believe it had units in a number of locations in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: A number. Could you be a bit more precise because a number could be three or four, but also 10 or even more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not think I could be more precise; a number which would be more than three or four, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Then I would like to ask you. Were there Green Berets in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I do not know the answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Were there Green Berets in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My recollection is that I heard reports of Green Berets in Mostar, but for any kind of information about this, it is a long time ago and my recollection must be unsure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Were there Green Berets in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again I would give the same answer which is that my recollection is that there might have been, but I have no, at this time several years later, I have no firm recollection of the reports of any of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Were there Green Berets in Jajce?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And again I would give the same answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Were there green berets in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again I would give the same answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again I would give the same answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: In Maglaj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again I would give the same answer with a greater degree of certainty in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: In Bihac, Dr. Gow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again I would give the same kind of answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Were there in Gornji Vakuf, I do not know whether I pronounce it right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again I would give the same kind of answer. There might have been, it is not unreasonable that there might have been but I really have no strong recollection any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Were there in Gorazde, Dr. Gow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again I would give the same answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Were there in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Sarajevo, I can be fairly sure that there were, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I try to count, Dr. Gow, and I was trying to get three or four. Could you please say, because I did not come to three or four places where they were. Could you then tell me where these three or four places were? Sarajevo is one and I think Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I am not sure which three or four you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I asked you whether they were spread all over the place or just in a few places because you talked about a number of places.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I asked you three or four or 10 because "it was a number" is a bit vague for me. I think you said: "Well, I would come to three or four", but when asking you and I just tried to -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may, my memory is that that is not what I said; what I said was several, certainly more than three or four.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Certainly more than three or four?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was my memory of what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: OK. My question would be, could you give me the other places, even going further than three or four, because I do understand that on Sarajevo you are quite clear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On Sarajevo, I was quite clear and on Maglaj, my memory is fairly strong, and I would also say that I presume the list you indicated is areas in which you have seen reports that Green Berets were present, and I find nothing particularly to disagree with that. I simply say that I cannot confirm that that was the case. The Green Berets, the Green Beret organisation, had been formed and was present in several locations which I indicated would be more than three or four. I am not sure what it is that you are asking me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I am asking what locations they were and since you said there might be three or four, so I am trying to find out whether you know what locations this was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again my memory is that I already said that I could not specify locations in response to the first question you asked me in this part of the questioning, and if my memory is wrong then I will say it now, that that was the case, that the Green Beret organisation had been formed and was present in parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I no longer have a specific recollection for the most part of which areas they were to be found in.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think what happened, if I may interrupt, Mr. Orie read off a list of places and asked you whether you knew whether Green Berets were in those places; you said yes to some and you did not know. What he wants you to do, I think, is to recapitulate, is that correct, and now state of that list which ones he can affirm that Green Berets were in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: If they were not in most of the places I mentioned, and if the witness has testified, as I understood it -- I may be wrong and then I would be glad to be corrected in my wrong understanding -- it was my impression that he said that there were at least at three or four places in Bosnia-Herzegovinan territory there were Green Berets. So I tried to find out where they were. I mentioned this list and I did not get out more than one or perhaps two. So I am curious to know where the other locations were where the Green Berets could be located since Dr. Gow said that there would be at least three or four which I understood as, perhaps, even more than three or four.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you find a question in that? Of the list that Mr. Orie read out, do you recall being able to indicate that there were Green Berets in more than one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I could ----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: And certainly how many?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I could recall my answer, which was with the exception of Sarajevo and possibly Maglaj, that I did not exclude the possibility that there were Green Berets in any of those areas. My recollection of my answer was that I have no longer a firm recollection, but I would regard it as not being unreasonable to judge that there might have been Green Berets organised in those areas. If my memory of what I said is wrong, then forgive me but I am fairly clear that that is what I said. So I was not saying that -- my answer was not that -- my answer was that they were in several places in response to your question, that that was more than three or four places, but in the nature of it, I do not recall specific locations in which they were to be found with the exception of Sarajevo where it was significantly to be noted. Forgive me, but I think maybe I was not clear enough maybe in the way I gave the answer in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. The second part of your answer saying, "at least in Sarajevo and probably in Maglaj", and yet you say, "I do not exclude that they might have been in these other places as well". The first part of your answer, in my recollection, was that there were at least three or four places where they were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My recollection of what I said was that they were in several places which would be more than three or four, but that I could not specify five years afterwards what those places were. But I do not see any problem -- but I do not see any problem in acknowledging that it is possible that they were in some of the places that you indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I will leave it. I will make my list longer than with two places. Are you aware of their presence in Prijedor the, Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say now that I am aware of their presence in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And again I cannot say that I am aware of their presence in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, I would like to -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But if I may just say that is on the same basis as I gave the answers to the previous questions, which was that five years afterwards it is very hard to remember exactly precise details of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course I do understand that it is difficult for you to remind exactly where they might have been. As far as the paramilitary groups are concerned, I would like to ask you a few questions on what you know about events happening in Gorazde. Could you first tell us where is Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Gorazde is in the southern, south-eastern part of Bosnia and Herzegovina, running along more or less the bottom, at the point that runs from along the bottom right-hand corner, the access going from the border of Serbia across the point of the border of Serbia and Montenegro and down to the Adriatic Sea. Gorazde is located along that access.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, what was the ethnic situation in Gorazde? Was there a Muslim majority, a Serb majority, a Croatian majority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: But the population -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My recollection or, rather, I am not sure, but I am aware that it was generally reported as being a predominantly Muslim town.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: A Muslim town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is conventionally reported as being a predominantly Muslim town, but I am not aware off the top of my head of the specific figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Was there a Serb minority in that town, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: There was a Serb minority. Do you know whether the Mayor was a Serb, a Muslim, a Croat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am afraid I am not an expert in Bosnian local government so I cannot answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Are you aware of any imprisonment by the Mayor of Gorazde, imprisonment of Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of that. I am no more expert in local Bosnian criminal or criminal related activity than local government.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I am aware that you might not be able to answer the question, but I nevertheless would like to put it to you because it might be that at some specific aspect you might know the answer. Are you aware of the police being taken over by the Muslim government of Gorazde, as far as you can speak about a government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I am not aware of that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to Gorazde later on? I am not talking about local government any more, but was Gorazde ever taken by Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serbian forces entered the town of Gorazde in April 1994. The town of Gorazde -----

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Dr. Gow, if you will allow me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Forgive me, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I tried to concentrate my questioning on the situation we were talking about, preparing for the war and that is where I started, paramilitary groups, whether these were groups that were active in preparing for the war in 1991 and 1992. So I would like to know your answer about, let us say, the period of two years afterwards. That is what I am interested in to know at this moment. So whether Gorazde was taken up to, let us say, mid 93?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, could you -----
